## Course description

Bayesian parameter estimation and hypothesis testing offer a useful alternative to the classic frequentist paradigm within psychological science. This class will cover the foundations of Bayesian inference and hypothesis testing with the primary emphasis on fitting multiple regression and multi-level models common within psychology. A variety of response distributions will be discussed: Gaussian, binary and count, ordinal, survival, probability, and zero-inflated models, among others. Topics include: model calibration, regularization, prior and posterior predictions, Bayes factors, missing data, Bayesian power, cross-validation, Bayesian meta-analysis, distributional models, and multivariate response models.  

<br>  

## Course learning objectives

1.  Take what you know (regression) and do it Bayesian (and more!)

2.  Know the advantages of Bayesian data analysis

3.  Rethink your approach to statistical modeling and inference


## Class textbook

- McElreath, R. (2020). Statistical Rethinking: A Bayesian Course with Examples in R. SECOND EDITION CRC Press. 

Note that McElreath also has lectures from his book posted on his YouTube. They are excellent. While some bits of the class materials are covered in his lectures I believe the content of this course and his course complement one another. His focus is making the content digestible, viewing the broader picture, and delving into philosophy of science more so. We will focus more on the applied aspects, using specific programs and making sure we are comfortable "doing" the work rather than just understanding it at the high level. 

Please check them out, especially if you are lost: 
https://tinyurl.com/yckrrzjy

Solomon Kurz has also created a book that does all of the examples in brms. https://bookdown.org/content/4857/ It is extremely helpful. He focuses on brms helper functions, some of which are deprecated, and we will mainly focus on tidybayes, and marginaleffects, but to get an idea of how to apply the content this book is extremely useful. *I highly recommend you read this along with the corresponding chapter from SR.*  

We will also read some chapters from Model to Meaning (M2M) by Vincent Arel-Bundock, who created the marginaleffects package:
https://marginaleffects.com

Andrew Heiss has some nice blog posts that cover the marginaleffects package and walk through in great detail some difficult topics. 

AH #1: https://www.andrewheiss.com/blog/2022/09/26/guide-visualizing-types-posteriors/  
AH #2: https://www.andrewheiss.com/blog/2022/05/20/marginalia/  
AH #3: https://www.andrewheiss.com/blog/2022/11/29/conditional-marginal-marginaleffects/  


*Recommended text (not required)*

- Kruschke, J. (2015). Doing Bayesian Data Analysis. SECOND EDITION. 

(This is more of a traditional stats textbook from a psychologist. It is more comprehensive but less readable. Some practices are no longer standard, the structure of the book isn't how I would present everything and it misses some important developments since it came out in 2015. Yes, a book from 2015 is now wildly out of date in this field. That said I still use it often as a reference).

Solomon also has a brms-based walkthrough of Kruschke: https://bookdown.org/content/3686/

- Farrell, S., & Lewandowsky, S. (2018). Computational modeling of cognition and behavior. Cambridge University Press

(Very good for those who predominantly do cognitive models/behavioral tasks. These are more advanced models that we will touch on at the end of the semester, however, go ahead and read this earlier if you are inclined.)

- Gelman, A., Hill, J., & Vehtari, A. (2020). Regression and other stories. Cambridge University Press. 

(A practical compendium of how to approach GLMs. If you feel like you need a refresher on GLM or are lost at any point in the semester with concepts you feel like "should have" learned prior, this book will help. Very readable. It is Bayesian but also not, focusing more on regression basics.)

- Lee, M. D., & Wagenmakers, E. J. (2014). Bayesian cognitive modeling: A practical course. Cambridge University Press 

(Terse but technically correct intro of Bayesian stats, best for completing your collection of Bayesian books by psychologists. I would not recommend as an intro book)

## Grading

No exams this year. Your grade has two parts:

| Component | Weight |
|-----------|--------|
| Weekly homework (13 assignments, lowest one dropped) | 70% |
| Final project | 30% |

### Homework

There is homework (almost) every week, just to keep you doing something with the material every week. Some weeks it's a quick check that takes under an hour; other weeks it's a full analysis. Each homework counts equally, and your lowest homework score is dropped. A homework you skip counts as a zero, so that's the one that gets dropped.

Homework is mostly applied computation, often with your own data. You may work on homework together in groups, but everyone turns in their own write-up.

- **Posted** Thursday after class; **due** the following Thursday at 2:30 pm (start of class) on Canvas. The homework spanning spring break is due the Thursday after break.
- **Turn in two files:** your `.qmd` and the rendered `.html`. Start from the [homework template](hw-template.qmd){download="hw-template.qmd"}, which sets things up so the `.html` is one self-contained file with your code showing.
- **Late homework** loses 10% of its points for each day (or part of a day) it's late, counted from the original due date. One day late, the best you can get is 90%; five days late, 50%; ten days late, nothing.

I use AI (in line with the policy below) to help with a first pass at grading: checking that code runs, that models match the question, and drafting feedback. I review everything and assign every grade myself.

### Final project

The final project is a series of models and visualizations using your own data. We (you and Josh) will work together to go over what your data are, and what sort of analyses, checks and visualizations you should do. The sooner in the semester you have these conversations with me, the better. By week 6 (Feb 23) you need to have a plan approved. The project is due during finals week.

**Grades**:

| Final % | Grade |
|---------|-------|
| 100 | A+ |
| 92 to <100 | A |
| 90 to <92 | A− |
| 89 to <90 | B+ |
| 81 to <89 | B |
| 80 to <81 | B− |
| 70 to <80 | C |
| 60 to <70 | D |
| below 60 | F |

## AI overlord helpers

AI tools (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Copilot, Positron Assistant, and whatever shows up next month) are rapidly changing how we write code. They are truly wonderful for writing code quickly (rather than going down crazy rabbit holes), and they're used constantly outside of the classroom, including for R. It would be CRAZY not to incorporate them into your learning.

That said, they still give you wrong code, and with Bayesian models the wrong code often runs just fine: a prior on the wrong scale, a `brms` formula that isn't the model you think it is, a marginaleffects call that averages over the wrong thing. My goal is to get you to a place where you can use these tools and tell whether what they hand you gives the right answer or the wrong one. Here is my policy for this class:

1. You are allowed to use any AI tool on homework and the take-home project.
2. If you do, say so: which tool, and what you used it for. Include the prompt, or a link to the shared chat if you had a back and forth conversation.
3. You own every line you turn in. If you can't explain what a line of code does and why it's there, it shouldn't be there.

Disclosing this helps make sure you understand why the code works or doesn't. It also lets me learn what does and does not work when communicating with our AI overlords.
